title: Redundant Delegation at Method, Class, or Layer Boundaries
pattern: Delegation reproduces an underlying interface without adding domain behavior, checks, transformation, or a meaningful isolation boundary. Diagnose the redundant method, the middle-man class, or the traversed layer chain separately.
why_bad: Unnecessary interfaces and indirection make modules shallower, obscure the actual flow of control, and force every signature change in the lower layer to be propagated upward. Whole-class or multi-layer repetition multiplies boilerplate and maintenance surface; any actual runtime or compilation overhead depends on the implementation rather than being guaranteed.
detection: Method/adjacent-layer case: a public method or multi-tier wrapper whose body consists solely of a single call to the adjacent object's matching method, with equivalent arguments and signature and no local operations or checks. Class case: all or a vast majority of a struct's public methods (e.g., greater than 80%) do nothing but forward arguments and return values to an internal field object without transformation. Architecture case: trace a request through multiple physical modules or layers (e.g., `web` -> `domain` -> `db`) and confirm matching-signature forwarding with no intermediate business rules or transformations. One forwarding method does not establish either broader case.
counterexample: `Context-dependent`. Implementing a required trait (e.g. `Deref`) where delegation is structurally mandatory; a facade that groups and simplifies access to a complex multi-object subsystem or isolates a volatile third-party library; a proxy/decorator adding genuine dynamic concerns such as logging or security; and physical deployment boundaries where strict security checks, RPC marshaling, or cross-network serialization are required.
fix: For a single pass-through method, let the caller invoke the underlying object's method directly, or merge the adjacent layers if their responsibilities heavily overlap. Remove a middle-man class (Remove Middle Man) only when its overall responsibility is redundant. For a pass-through chain, adopt an "open" layered style that lets simple requests bypass intermediate layers, or collapse truly redundant layers, while retaining required checks and deployment boundaries. If the wrapper constructs its delegate, account for that construction/lifetime behavior before replacing it.
source: John K. Ousterhout, *A Philosophy of Software Design* (2018), Chapter 7 ("Different Layer, Different Abstraction - Pass-Through Methods"), pp. 46, 310–313; Martin Fowler et al., *Refactoring: Improving the Design of Existing Code* (1999), Chapter 3 ("Bad Smells in Code - Middle Man"), pp. 110, 259–260; Steve McConnell, *Code Complete* (2004), Chapter 24; Mark Richards & Neal Ford, *Fundamentals of Software Architecture* (2020), Chapter 10 ("Layered Architecture Style - Architecture Sinkhole"), p. 138.
